title: Tired and pale
stem: 52-year-old man, tired for 3 months, short of breath on stairs. Stool test found hidden blood.
opts: Iron deficiency from slow GI blood loss
why: Low hemoglobin with a LOW MCV = microcytic anemia. A HIGH RDW means the red cells vary a lot in size, typical of iron deficiency (thalassemia trait usually has a normal RDW). Mildly high platelets are common in iron deficiency. In an adult, iron deficiency means looking for bleeding, so the next step is scoping the gut (colonoscopy/endoscopy).
pearl: Microcytic: think iron deficiency, thalassemia, chronic disease. High RDW points to iron.

title: Numb feet and tired
stem: 61-year-old woman with tingling feet, unsteady walking and a sore red tongue.
why: Low hemoglobin with a very HIGH MCV = macrocytic (megaloblastic) anemia. Add nerve symptoms (tingling, poor position sense) and it points to B12 deficiency: B12 is needed for DNA synthesis and for myelin. Pernicious anemia is autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor, so B12 can't be absorbed in the ileum. Folate deficiency also raises MCV but does NOT cause nerve damage.
pearl: Macrocytic + neuro signs = B12 until proven otherwise.

title: Fever and cough
stem: 68-year-old man with fever, shaking chills and a cough with rusty sputum for 2 days.
why: High WBC driven by NEUTROPHILS (neutrophilia) is the classic response to bacterial infection. A viral infection more often raises lymphocytes, allergy raises eosinophils, and CLL raises lymphocytes massively. With fever and rusty sputum this fits bacterial pneumonia (often Streptococcus pneumoniae).
pearl: Neutrophils = bacteria. Lymphocytes = viruses. Eosinophils = allergy/parasites.

title: Tiny red dots
stem: 9-year-old boy with tiny red dots on his legs and easy bruising, 2 weeks after a cold. Otherwise well.
why: ONLY the platelets are low; red cells and white cells are normal. Isolated low platelets in a well child after a viral illness = immune thrombocytopenia: antibodies coat platelets and the spleen removes them. Leukemia usually knocks down several cell lines. Hemophilia is a clotting factor problem with NORMAL platelets.
pearl: Petechiae = platelet problem. Deep joint bleeds = clotting factor problem.

title: Thirsty and vomiting
stem: 13-year-old with 2 weeks of thirst, peeing a lot and weight loss, now vomiting and breathing deep and fast.
why: Very high glucose + low bicarbonate + HIGH anion gap (134 − 98 − 9 = 27) = high anion gap metabolic acidosis from ketones. No insulin means fat is burned into ketoacids. Potassium looks high but total body potassium is actually LOW: acidosis and lack of insulin shift potassium out of cells. Deep fast breathing is Kussmaul breathing, blowing off CO2. Treatment: fluids, insulin, potassium replacement.
pearl: Anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO3). Normal about 8–12.

title: Barely peeing
stem: 74-year-old man, barely passing urine for 2 days after a bad stomach bug; he kept taking his blood pressure pills.
why: BUN and creatinine both well above range = the kidneys aren't filtering. When filtration drops, potassium (6.3, dangerous for the heart) and acid build up, so bicarbonate falls. Dehydration plus blood pressure drugs that reduce kidney blood flow (like ACE inhibitors) is a classic setup. High potassium needs an ECG right away (peaked T waves).
pearl: Creatinine is the filtration marker. High K⁺ is the emergency.

title: Hot day, dry mouth
stem: 82-year-old woman found confused at home after a heat wave, very dry mouth.
why: High sodium (hypernatremia) means too little water relative to salt. BUN rising much more than creatinine (ratio about 31, above 20) suggests a "pre-renal" picture: low blood flow to the kidneys, not kidney damage. Older adults feel less thirst, so heat waves are dangerous. Water must be replaced SLOWLY: fixing sodium too fast can swell the brain.

title: Confused after meningitis
stem: 45-year-old man recovering from meningitis becomes confused and has a seizure.
why: Low sodium (hyponatremia) with low BUN in someone who isn't dehydrated. Brain problems (meningitis, bleeds, injury) and some lung diseases can trigger SIADH: too much antidiuretic hormone makes the kidney keep water, diluting sodium. Low sodium makes brain cells swell, causing confusion and seizures. Treatment starts with fluid restriction, and sodium must be corrected slowly.
pearl: Low sodium + brain or lung disease → think SIADH.

title: Weak and sleepy
stem: 30-year-old with Guillain-Barré syndrome whose breathing muscles are getting weak; now drowsy.
opts: Metabolic acidosis from lactic acid buildup
why: pH low = acidosis. PaCO2 high = the lungs aren't blowing off CO2 (hypoventilation), so this is a RESPIRATORY acidosis. Bicarbonate is only slightly up because the kidneys take days to compensate (acute). Weak breathing muscles in Guillain-Barré can need a ventilator, so doctors track breathing strength closely.
pearl: Step 1 pH, step 2 CO2 (lungs), step 3 HCO3 (kidneys/metabolism).

title: Sudden breathless
stem: 34-year-old woman with sudden sharp chest pain and breathlessness after a long flight. Breathing fast.
why: pH high = alkalosis. PaCO2 LOW = breathing fast blows off CO2 → RESPIRATORY alkalosis. Low oxygen plus a long flight raises concern for a pulmonary embolism (a clot in the lung arteries). Panic attacks also cause respiratory alkalosis but with normal oxygen.
pearl: Fast breathing → CO2 down → pH up.

title: Deep breathing teen
stem: 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes who missed insulin, vomiting, deep sighing breaths.
why: pH low = acidosis. Bicarbonate very low = METABOLIC acidosis. PaCO2 is low because the lungs are compensating: breathing deep and fast (Kussmaul) to blow off acid as CO2. Winter's formula predicts the CO2 for full compensation: 1.5 × 8 + 8 = 20 (±2), and 22 fits.

title: Vomiting for days
stem: 19-year-old with 4 days of non-stop vomiting from a stomach bug, weak and dizzy.
opts: Metabolic alkalosis from losing stomach acid
Metabolic acidosis from diarrhea losing bicarbonate
Respiratory acidosis from an opioid overdose
why: pH high = alkalosis. Bicarbonate high = METABOLIC alkalosis. Vomiting loses hydrochloric acid from the stomach, leaving the body with extra base. The lungs compensate a bit by breathing slower (CO2 slightly up). Diarrhea does the opposite: it loses bicarbonate and causes metabolic ACIDOSIS.

title: Yellow after a trip
stem: 24-year-old back from a trip, a week of nausea and fever, now his eyes are yellow.
opts: Gallstone blocking the common bile duct
why: ALT and AST in the THOUSANDS = liver cells are being destroyed (hepatocellular injury). ALP is only slightly up, so this is not mainly a blockage. Hepatitis A spreads by contaminated food and water, is common in travellers, and usually clears on its own. Normal albumin means the liver's making protein fine, so the injury is new.
pearl: ALT/AST up = liver cell injury. ALP/GGT up = bile flow (cholestatic) problem.

title: Yellow and itchy
stem: 58-year-old with yellow skin, very itchy, pale stools and dark urine. Pain under the right ribs after fatty meals.
opts: Gallstone blocking the common bile duct
why: ALP and GGT far higher than ALT/AST = CHOLESTATIC pattern (bile can't drain). Mostly DIRECT (conjugated) bilirubin: the liver processed it but can't get it out, so it spills into urine (dark) and doesn't reach the gut (pale stools). Bile salts in the skin cause itching. Next step: ultrasound, then ERCP to remove the stone.
pearl: Pale stools + dark urine + itch = blocked bile flow.

title: Yellow when sick
stem: 17-year-old whose eyes go slightly yellow when he skips meals or has a cold. Feels fine otherwise.
why: Only bilirubin is up, and it's the INDIRECT (unconjugated) kind; all liver enzymes are normal. Gilbert syndrome is a common harmless genetic quirk: the enzyme UGT1A1 that conjugates bilirubin works at reduced capacity, so fasting, stress or illness makes mild jaundice. No treatment needed.
pearl: Isolated indirect bilirubin + normal enzymes in a well teen = Gilbert.

title: Kidney patient feels weak
stem: 66-year-old with long-term kidney disease, missed dialysis, now weak with an odd heartbeat.
why: Potassium 7.1 is dangerous: it changes the resting voltage of heart cells and can cause peaked T waves, wide QRS and cardiac arrest. Kidneys normally remove potassium, so missed dialysis lets it build up (and urea, creatinine and acid). Emergency care: calcium to protect the heart membrane, then insulin with glucose to push potassium into cells, then removal (dialysis).
pearl: High K⁺: protect the heart (calcium), shift it (insulin), remove it.
